artist.artist_description: Patti Page, an American singer born in 1927 in Oklahoma, was known for her versatile voice that spanned genres like traditional pop, country, and jazz. She rose to fame in the late 1940s with hits like "Tennessee Waltz," which became one of the best-selling singles of the 20th century, and throughout her career, she earned 14 top-10 Billboard hits and three Grammy nominations. A trivia note about Page is that she was often referred to as "The Singin' Rage, Miss Patti Page" and was the first to record an overdubbed vocal, a technique that became standard in music production.

Hank Williams was an American singer-songwriter known for his contributions to country music. Born in 1923 in Alabama, he rose to fame in the late 1940s with hits like "Lovesick Blues" and "I'm So Lonesome I Could Cry." He was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame posthumously in 1961, and trivia includes that his son, Hank Williams Jr., also became a successful country musician.

Kitty Wells, born in Nashville, Tennessee, was an American country music singer known as the "Queen of Country Music." She rose to fame with her 1952 hit "It Wasn't God Who Made Honky Tonk Angels," becoming the first female country singer to have a number one hit. Wells was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1976 and continued performing into her 80s, leaving a lasting impact on the genre.

Jim Reeves, an American country and pop singer born in 1923, rose to fame in the 1950s with his smooth, velvety voice, earning the nickname "Gentleman Jim." His hits like "He'll Have to Go" and "Welcome to My World" crossed over from country to pop charts, showcasing his broad appeal. Tragically, Reeves died in a plane crash in 1964 at the height of his career, but his music continues to influence and be celebrated in the genre.

The Davis Sisters were an American country music duo from near Philadelphia, consisting of sisters Skeeter and Betty Jack Davis. They gained fame in the 1950s with hits like "I Forgot More Than You'll Ever Know," which became a classic in the genre. Tragically, Betty Jack died in a car accident in 1953, after which Skeeter continued as a solo artist.

Webb Pierce was an American country music artist born in 1921 in West Monroe, Louisiana. He rose to fame in the 1950s with hits like "There Stands the Glass" and "In the Jailhouse Now," becoming one of the genre's top stars and known for his flamboyant style, including his famous guitar-shaped swimming pool. Pierce was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2001, reflecting his significant impact on the genre.

Eddy Arnold was an American country music singer born in 1918 in Tennessee, who began his career in the 1940s after performing on radio stations and joining the Grand Ole Opry. Known as "The Tennessee Plowboy," he achieved significant success with hits like "Make the World Go Away" and "Bouquet of Roses," becoming one of the best-selling country artists of all time with over 85 million records sold. Arnold was also the first country artist to perform at Carnegie Hall and was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1966.

George Jones was an American country music singer known for his distinctive voice and emotive performances. Born in Texas in 1931, he began singing in church and on the radio as a child, eventually rising to fame with hits like "He Stopped Loving Her Today," which is often considered one of the greatest country songs ever recorded. Jones won numerous awards, including multiple Grammys, and was known for his tumultuous personal life and struggles with substance abuse, earning him the nickname "No Show Jones" for missing performances.

Tennessee Ernie Ford was an American singer and television host known for his bass-baritone voice and his work in the country, pop, and gospel genres. Born in 1919 in Bristol, Tennessee, he gained fame with his 1955 hit "Sixteen Tons," which became a crossover success, reaching No. 1 on both the pop and country charts. Ford also hosted his own variety show, "The Ford Show," and was awarded a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 1990.

Patsy Cline was an American singer known for her contributions to country music. Born in Virginia in 1932, she rose to fame in the 1950s with hits like "Walkin' After Midnight" and "Crazy," the latter written by Willie Nelson. Cline tragically died in a plane crash at age 30, but her powerful voice and emotional delivery continue to influence artists across genres.

Sonny James, an American country music singer and songwriter, was born in Hackleburg, Alabama, and rose to fame in the 1950s. Known as the "Southern Gentleman," he achieved significant success with 26 consecutive No. 1 hits on the Billboard country charts from 1967 to 1971, a record at the time. Interestingly, James also had a brief career in baseball before dedicating himself to music.

Ferlin Husky was an American country music singer born in Missouri in 1925. He gained fame in the 1950s with hits like "Gone" and "Wings of a Dove," the latter becoming a gospel standard. Husky was known for his versatility, performing in various genres including country, pop, and comedy under the stage name Simon Crum.

Marty Robbins was an American singer, songwriter, and NASCAR driver, best known for his contributions to the country and western genres. Born in Arizona in 1925, he began his music career in the late 1940s, achieving fame with hits like "El Paso," which won him a Grammy Award in 1961. Interestingly, Robbins was also an avid race car driver, competing in NASCAR events and even releasing a song about his racing experiences titled "Crash Course in the Blues."

Bobby Helms was an American singer known for his work in country and rockabilly music. Born in 1933 in Indiana, he rose to fame with his 1957 hit "Jingle Bell Rock," which became a Christmas classic. Helms was also a talented yodeler and continued to perform and record until his death in 1997.

Don Gibson was an American country music singer-songwriter born in 1928 in North Carolina, known for pioneering the Nashville sound. He gained fame in the 1950s and 1960s with hits like "Oh Lonesome Me" and "I Can't Stop Loving You," the latter covered by Ray Charles. Gibson was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2001, and interestingly, he wrote over 150 songs during his career.

Ray Price was an American country music singer, songwriter, and guitarist known for his contributions to the genre, particularly in the development of the "Ray Price Shuffle." Born in 1926 in Texas, he began his career in the late 1940s and achieved fame with hits like "Crazy Arms" and "For the Good Times." Price was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1996 and continued performing until his death in 2013.

Johnny Horton was an American country and rockabilly singer born in 1925 in Los Angeles, California. He gained fame in the 1950s with hits like "The Battle of New Orleans," which won a Grammy Award for Best Country & Western Recording in 1960. Tragically, Horton died in a car crash in 1960 at the age of 35, leaving behind a legacy as one of the pioneers of the rockabilly genre.

Tex Williams, an American musician, was a prominent figure in the Western swing and country genres. Born in 1917 in Illinois, he gained fame with his band, the Western Caravan, and hit songs like "Smoke! Smoke! Smoke! (That Cigarette)." Interestingly, Williams was known for his trademark white Stetson hat and his smooth, baritone voice.

The Weavers were an American folk music quartet formed in 1948 in New York City, known for popularizing folk music during the late 1940s and early 1950s. Their early success came with hits like "Goodnight, Irene" and "Kisses Sweeter Than Wine," which helped bring folk music to mainstream audiences. Despite being blacklisted during the McCarthy era for their left-wing political affiliations, The Weavers were later recognized with a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2006.

Hank Snow was a Canadian country music artist born in 1914 in Nova Scotia. He began performing at a young age and gained fame with songs like "I'm Moving On," which became a No. 1 hit in 1950. Snow was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1979, and interestingly, he was known for his unique "yodeling" style.

Stuart Hamblen was an American singer and songwriter known for his work in the country and gospel genres. Born in 1908 in Texas, he began his career as a radio personality before transitioning to music, where he became famous for songs like "This Ole House" and "It Is No Secret (What God Can Do)." Hamblen was also notable for being the first artist to have a number one hit on the Billboard country charts and for his conversion to Christianity, which influenced his later work.

Leon Payne was an American country music singer and songwriter born in 1917 in Alba, Texas. He began his career in the 1930s and is best known for writing the classic song "I Love You Because," which has been covered by numerous artists. Payne was blind since childhood and was inducted into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame in 1970.

George Morgan was an American country music singer born in 1924 in Tennessee. He gained fame with his 1949 hit "Candy Kisses," which became his signature song and a country classic. Morgan was known for his smooth baritone voice and was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame posthumously in 1998.

track.intro: Kicking off at number 1 in the 1950s, the country classic 'The Tennessee Waltz' by Patti Page sweeps us into a dance!

'The Tennessee Waltz' not only topped the charts but also became the first song to reach a million in sales by a female artist. And that's the magic that still spins on turntables today!
